2022_240_m021522bdmtg.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held February 15, 2022 at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:00 p.m. before an audience of approximately 80. The Board adopted resolutions 22-015 through 22-026, each on a 7 to 0 vote, covering Principal Appreciation Month, the consent agenda, a new hire, open-enrollment closures, Schools of Choice numbers, several construction and technology awards, an IDEA Full Funding Act resolution, and a MASB ballot. The largest single action was the Site Work Paving Program awarded to Nagle Paving at a total of $2,048,607.75 from the Building Site Sinking Fund and Capital Projects Fund. The meeting adjourned at 9:03 p.m.

**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, February 15, 2022, Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Also present: Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson; Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Fulcher, and West. Approximately 80 members of the audience attended. Adjourned 9:03 p.m. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary.

**Recognitions**
Fall 2021 All-State Athletes were named across boys tennis, boys soccer, and girls golf. Athletic Director Tim Fulcher recognized the Troy High School Boys Tennis Team as MHSAA Division 1 State Champions for fall 2021 and presented certificates. The Board honored Melissa Verduyn, Systems Analyst/Admin Webmaster, for artwork visualizing the District pillars of World Class; Kerry Birmingham introduced her and presented a framed photograph of her artwork plus a certificate of appreciation.

**Resolutions and Votes** (all 7 Yes, 0 No)

| No. | Subject | Moved / Supported |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 22-015 | February as Principal Appreciation Month | Philippart / Hammond |
| 22-016 | Consent agenda items A-D | Hauff / Anne |
| 22-017 | Personnel, new hire Samantha Morgan | Wilson / Hauff |
| 22-018 | Schools closed to open enrollment 2022-2023 | Anne / Gottlieb |
| 22-019 | Schools of Choice 105 and 105c | Philippart / Anne |
| 22-020 | Site Work Paving Program | Anne / Hauff |
| 22-021 | Asbestos abatement | Wilson / Hammond |
| 22-022 | Network firewall replacement | Hammond / Gottlieb |
| 22-023 | Fiber connectivity to TLC | Gottlieb / Philippart |
| 22-024 | Replacement ovens, Athens | Hammond / Anne |
| 22-025 | IDEA Full Funding Act resolution | Hauff / Wilson |
| 22-026 | 2022 MASB Board of Directors ballot | Philippart / Anne |

**Consent Agenda (22-016)**
Minutes of the January 4, 2022 Workshop; minutes of the January 18, 2022 Organizational and Regular Meeting; Treasurer's Report for December 2021; and cancellation of the March 12, 2022 Winter Retreat with the July 19 Board Meeting rescheduled to July 26, 2022 at 9:00 a.m.

**Enrollment Actions**
22-018 closed Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, and Boulan Park Schools, plus Athens and Troy High Schools, to open enrollment for 2022-2023, excepting not more than twenty-five (25) incoming ninth grade students residing in the Troy High attendance area who wish to attend Athens; siblings currently in grades 9-11 at Athens and Troy High may remain. 22-019 accepted a Limited Schools of Choice program under Section 105 and 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996 for eighteen (18) kindergarten, three (3) first grade, and sixteen (16) total 6th-8th grade nonresident students.

**Business Awards**

| Item | Vendor | Amount | Fund |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Site Work Paving Program | Nagle Paving | $2,048,607.75 total | Building Site Sinking Fund and Capital Projects Fund |
| Asbestos abatement | Quality Environmental | $85,600.00 | Capital Projects Fund |
| Network firewall replacement | Delta Networks | $343,720.69 total | 2019 Capital Projects Fund |
| Fiber connectivity | Fiber Link, Inc. | $137,562.60 total | 2019 Capital Projects Fund |
| Two UNOX ovens | Stafford Smith | $58,524.00 | Food Service Fund |

**Public Communication**
No comment on agenda items. Twelve speakers addressed non-agenda items, raising equity versus equality, classroom volunteers, curriculum, media center content, diversity and inclusion, mask mandates and their lifting, and library books.

**Other**
22-025 supported the IDEA Full Funding Act. 22-026 cast the District ballot for Melandie Hines, Wayne Westland Community Schools, Region 8, three-year term, on the 2022 MASB Board of Directors. President Schmidt announced the next Board Workshop for March 1st at 6:00 p.m. and the next Board Meeting for March 15th at 7:00 p.m., both at the Services Building.
2022_240_m021522bdmtg.verbose:
Official minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held February 15, 2022 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Fulcher, and West. There were approximately 80 members of the audience. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, and bear the initials GH/jh.

RECOGNITION - ALL-STATE ATHLETES FALL 2021. The following students received the distinction of being named All-State Athletes in their respective sports: Srihari Ananthalwan (Boys Tennis), Aiden Baraiac (Boys Soccer), Derek Blackwell (Boys Tennis), Matthew Gawthrop (Boys Soccer), Rintaro Goda (Boys Tennis), Ryan Gruca (Boys Soccer), Mayank Gudi (Boys Tennis), Aryan Gupta (Boys Tennis), Olivia Hemmila (Girls Golf), John Palomino (Boys Soccer), Rishi Shetty (Boys Tennis), Nikhil Tatineni (Boys Tennis), Andrew Wang (Boys Tennis), Ava Weeks (Girls Golf), and Nicholas Worrell (Boys Soccer).

TROY HIGH BOYS TENNIS STATE CHAMPIONS. Director of Athletics Mr. Tim Fulcher recognized the Troy High School Boys Tennis Team for being named MHSAA Division 1 State Champions for the fall of 2021. Athletes called up to receive a certificate and congratulations were Haresh Anand (Sophomore), Srihari Ananthalwan (Junior), Pranav Bellad (Senior), Derek Blackwell (Sophomore), Yashwant Dubbaka (Junior), Aryan Gupta (Senior), Dhruv Gupta (Freshman), Sai Rushil Kagithala (Junior), Shalin Kakasani (Senior), KyungJin Kim (Sophomore), Nishit Palepu (Sophomore), Eric Rymkiewicz (Senior), Zachary Saad (Senior), Joshua Samuelsen (Sophomore), Rishi Shetty (Senior), Sachin Sridhar (Senior), Nikhil Tatineni (Senior), and Andrew Wang (Senior). Srihari Ananthalwan and Aryan Gupta were noted as Flight State Champions at #2 Doubles; Pranav Bellad and Zachary Saad were noted as Flight State Champions at #3 Doubles.

TSD MISSION MOMENT. The Board honored Melissa Verduyn, Systems Analyst/Admin Webmaster, who works in both the Technology Department and on the creative team. When the District began the process to evolve the characteristics of a world class school district, it ran into challenges producing a visual image similar to the pillars that could accurately communicate the vision; Verduyn brought it together in a way that helps the community understand and connect. Kerry Birmingham introduced Melissa, described her contributions, and presented her with a framed photograph of her artwork along with a certificate of appreciation.

PRINCIPAL APPRECIATION MONTH, RESOLUTION 22-015. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Hammond. The resolution recited that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools and districts are to ensure that all Troy students are college and career ready; that K-12 school principals play a vital role in student success and act as liaison between school and community; that Troy School District principals are dedicated, quality educational professionals; and that during February the District joins educators, parents and students throughout Michigan to raise awareness of the importance of educational leadership. It resolved that the Troy Board of Education officially recognizes February as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS: None. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS): None.

GENERAL CONSENT AGENDA, RESOLUTION 22-016. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne to approve items A, B, C, and D: minutes of the January 4, 2022 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the January 18, 2022 Board of Education Organizational and Regular Meeting; Treasurer's Report for December 2021; and cancellation of the March 12, 2022 Winter Retreat together with rescheduling of the July 19 Board Meeting to July 26, 2022, to be held at 9:00 a.m. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

PERSONNEL, RESOLUTION 22-017. Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Hauff to approve the elementary and secondary personnel recommendation, a new hire, Samantha Morgan. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

CURRICULUM - SCHOOLS CLOSED TO OPEN ENROLLMENT FOR 2022-2023, RESOLUTION 22-018. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Gottlieb, adopting a resolution to close Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park Schools as well as Athens and Troy High Schools to open enrollment for the 2022-2023 school year, with the exception of not more than twenty-five (25) incoming ninth grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School. Students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High and currently enrolled in grades 9 through 11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain for the 2022-2023 school year. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

SCHOOLS OF CHOICE REPORT. Ms. Griffor shared that the Board had the opportunity to review the Schools of Choice data and information at the March 1, 2022 Board of Education Workshop, and that the Board would be asked to pass a resolution approving the suggested Schools of Choice numbers for the 2022-2023 school year.

SCHOOLS OF CHOICE 105 AND 105C, RESOLUTION 22-019. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne. Exercising the option permitted by Section 105 and 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979, as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, the Board will accept applications for a Limited Schools of Choice program for the 2022-2023 school year for eighteen (18) kindergarten, three (3) first grade, and sixteen (16) total 6th through 8th grade nonresident students who attend a school district within or outside of Oakland County if that intermediate school district is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Mrs. Hammond commented that she appreciates the District bringing the number of Schools of Choice students down from what it was years ago.

BUSINESS - SITE WORK PAVING PROJECTS, RESOLUTION 22-020. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Hauff, awarding the Site Work Paving Program bid and approving the amount as an expenditure of the Building Site Sinking Fund and Capital Projects Fund. Nagle Paving: Hamilton (main parking lot and drives) $524,990.00; Martell (drains, paving and retention pond) $562,990.00; Wass (parking lot, receiving drive, entrance loop) $567,125.00; Facilities and Operations $295,950.00; Contingency $97,552.75; TOTAL $2,048,607.75. Vote: Yes 7, No 0. Mr. Hauff inquired as to when the paving projects would be completed; Mr. West indicated they should be finished by June 17th.

ASBESTOS ABATEMENT PROJECT, RESOLUTION 22-021. Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Hammond, awarding the asbestos abatement bid to Quality Environmental in the amount of $85,600.00, approved as an expenditure from the Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

NETWORK FIREWALL REPLACEMENT, RESOLUTION 22-022. Moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mr. Gottlieb, awarding the network firewall replacement and approving the amount as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. Delta Networks base bid $327,353.04; Contingency $16,367.65; TOTAL $343,720.69. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

FIBER CONNECTION TO TLC, RESOLUTION 22-023. Moved by Mr. Gottlieb and supported by Dr. Philippart, awarding fiber connectivity services and approving the amount as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. Fiber Link, Inc. base bid $74,562.60; Make Ready Allowance $63,000.00; TOTAL $137,562.60. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

REPLACEMENT OVENS - ATHENS, RESOLUTION 22-024. Moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mrs. Anne, awarding the purchase of two UNOX ovens to Stafford Smith in the amount of $58,524.00, approved as an expenditure of the Food Service Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

STUDENT REPRESENTATIVE REPORTS. Sarayu Bethamcherla reported for Troy High School; Alyssa McLarty for Troy College and Career High School; Yara Mashal for International Academy-East; and Sasha Palmkoeck for Athens High School.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). President Schmidt described how Public Participation would be conducted in compliance with the Open Meetings Act and reviewed the guidelines for public comment. Speakers: Mrs. Katie MacFarland, TSD parent and resident, on the difference between equity and equality; Kristina Sosnoski, TSD parent and resident, on allowing parents to volunteer in classrooms again; Mrs. Kacy Bailey, parent of two students, on curriculum being taught in the District; Mr. Ollie Apahidean, TSD parent, on media content in school media centers; Mr. Christopher Henne, TSD parent, on diversity, equity and inclusion and arming kids with tools to be good quality citizens; B.J. Lennon, TSD parent, on the mask mandates being lifted; Mrs. Diana Magiera, TSD parent, on mask enforcements and effects on children; Stephanie Margilaj, TSD parent, on explicit books in school libraries; Kelly Jones, TSD parent, on the use of pronouns as a way to show respect; Dr. Stephanie Mikulski, TSD parent, on the mask requirement being discontinued prematurely; Ms. Ashleigh Jennings, TSD parent, on lifting the mask mandate and whether past mitigation measures will be reinstated; and Susan Tompkins, TSD resident, on masks and how teachers struggle to help students read with masks on.

OTHER - RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF IDEA FULL FUNDING ACT, RESOLUTION 22-025. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Dr. Wilson. The resolution recited that the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act was first enacted in 1975 to help ensure all students with disabilities have access to a free appropriate public education; that with IDEA's enactment the United States Congress committed to fund up to 40 percent of the additional cost of special education, promising up to 40 percent of the national average per pupil expenditure, currently estimated at $13,828 by the U.S. Department of Education; that more than 45 years after enactment the current federal investment in IDEA is less than 14 percent; that Troy and many other districts educate a growing number of children with disabilities now numbering more than seven million; that districts face increased demand for greater resources, including for students with multiple disabilities whose individual education plans require more resources; and that with each increase in the IDEA child count boards adjust budgets, with some school districts dedicating forty percent or more of their general education budgets to special education services. The Board resolved to support the IDEA Full Funding Act authorizing a ten year plan to fully fund the federal share of IDEA, to urge Congress's strong bipartisan support and passage, and to remain committed to providing students with disabilities and their families the supports they need while acknowledging the intergovernmental partnership among local, state, and federal levels of government. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

2022 MASB BOARD OF DIRECTORS ELECTION, RESOLUTION 22-026. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne, casting the Board's ballot for Melandie Hines, Wayne Westland Community Schools, for Region 8, three-year term, on the 2022 Michigan Association of School Boards Board of Directors. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

BOARD MEMBER COMMENTS. Dr. Philippart thanked the principals for their work and dedication. Mrs. Hammond echoed the sentiment and suggested parents wanting to volunteer reach out to their building principals. Mr. Gottlieb gave a shout out to teachers and students for the Oakland Youth Innovation Lab Passion Projects. Mrs. Anne congratulated Teacher of the Year nominees and winners and mentioned visiting the STEMI truck at Troy High and student interest. Mr. Hauff announced that parents with a child who will be 5 by September 1, 2022 should enroll early for kindergarten. Dr. Wilson echoed other members and mentioned the STEMI truck and how high school students get middle school students excited about learning. Dr. Machesky congratulated the athletes, Melissa Verduyn, and the principals, noted the District celebrated four Teacher of the Year winners the prior weekend, and thanked the TFEE for its monetary award, the TEA for its support, and Suburban Collection for a 2-year auto lease. Mr. Schmidt gave a shout out to Bill Turner for organizing the STEMI truck visit, and announced the next Board Workshop for March 1st at 6:00 p.m. at the Services Building and the next Board Meeting for March 15th at 7:00 p.m., also at the Services Building.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 9:03 p.m.

**Document**
Arctic Wolf Networks proposal overview for Managed Detection and Response and Managed Security Awareness Training, dated 3/21/22, marked Classification: Public on the cover with interior slides marked Confidential. Presented to Beth Soggs (IT Director) and Alan Wilson (Network Manager); prepared by Nick Hankins (Account Executive, Arctic Wolf) and Chris Pittman (Sr. Systems Engineer, Arctic Wolf), with People Driven represented by Bryan Teipel (President) and Dave Benham (Solution Architect). Contents: Executive Summary, Current Assessment, Why Arctic Wolf, Security Risk Quantification, Pricing Proposal, Partnership and Enablement.

**Stated Problem**
Troy Schools has a distributed network across multiple physical buildings with most traffic backhauled to the central hub, making visibility and network traffic monitoring a challenge; multiple security tools are in place with limited staff to monitor and correlate alerts; and lack of a broad detection and response mechanism could prevent quick identification, containment and remediation of sophisticated threats. The proposal states that building a 24x7x365 cybersecurity team in-house is probably unrealistic given constrained resources.

MDR architecture scoped to 1200 Users, 12,500 Student Users, 100 Servers, 1 300 Series Sensor, and 90 Day Log Retention, with AWN301 sensors, an Arctic Wolf agent, and a named Concierge Security Team (CST). 2022_241_3_a_troy_school_district_mdr_ms.verbose:
Vendor sales deck from Arctic Wolf Networks, Inc. titled Managed Detection and Response and Managed Security Awareness Training Proposal Overview, dated 3/21/22 and carried on the Troy School District Board agenda as item 3.a. The cover slide is marked Classification: Public; most interior slides carry the notice Classification: Confidential with copyright lines for 2020 and 2021 Arctic Wolf Networks, Inc. Presented To: Beth Soggs, IT Director, and Alan Wilson, Network Manager. Prepared By: Nick Hankins, Account Executive, Arctic Wolf, and Chris Pittman, Sr. Systems Engineer, Arctic Wolf. People Driven, the partner organization, is represented by Bryan Teipel, President, and Dave Benham, Solution Architect. The proposal contents are enumerated as six sections: Executive Summary, Current Assessment, Why Arctic Wolf, Security Risk Quantification, Pricing Proposal, and Partnership and Enablement.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY. The strategic initiative is stated as Enhance Security and Visibility. The problem statement holds that Troy Schools has a distributed network across multiple physical buildings with most traffic backhauled to the central hub, making visibility across the environment and monitoring of network traffic a challenge; that Troy Schools has multiple security tools in place with limited staff to monitor and correlate alerts or identify and respond to potential malicious activity; and that a lack of a broad detection and response mechanism could prevent the ability to quickly identify, contain and remediate sophisticated threats. The desired outcomes are to operationalize a full-feature SIEM solution leveraging existing IT and security controls, to obtain a full-functioning cloud-integrated SOC service, and to leverage a service-based solution that can identify, evaluate, and provide quarantine and remediation guidance for threat indicators in real time. The proposed solution is Arctic Wolf's security operations as-a-concierge service ingesting Troy Schools environmental telemetry to perform 24x7x365 observations, investigations, and incident response guidance; an open, vendor-agnostic SIEM platform ingesting standardized log sources and live network traffic analysis; and three dedicated Security Operations FTEs using the Arctic Wolf Cloud Platform for proactive threat hunting and continuous improvement.

CURRENT ASSESSMENT. Current challenges reported from the Troy team: IT and security resources are constrained and the cost and complexity of building a 24x7x365 cybersecurity team in-house is probably unrealistic; endpoint and network security tools are in place and seasoned security professionals are desired for guidance in environmental hardening and continuous improvement; and there is interest in human-led, proactive threat hunting over basic alert-response services. Negative business impacts listed include risk from cyber attack, reactive response distracting burdened IT staff from existing initiatives, and inability to identify dormant vulnerabilities and threats. Value drivers are described as Benchmark Your Business, Team Enhancement, Faster Intrusion Detection, and Harden Your Environment, the latter via the CST evaluating vulnerability and risk data and presenting on-demand executive reports and personalized risk remediation plans.

SERVICE OFFERINGS. Managed Risk (Discover, Benchmark, Harden) is framed against the Center for Internet Security statement that 80% of breaches could have been prevented if the organization had met the top 5 CIS controls. Managed Detection and Response covers Detect, Respond, and Recover. Managed Cloud Monitoring covers Identify, Monitor, and Simplify, including unsecured S3 buckets and unauthorized cloud deployments, IaaS configuration risks, and SaaS indicators of compromise. Managed Security Awareness covers Engage, Measure, and Transform. A statistics band on the same slide prints the figures 47%, 80%, 85% and 70% alongside claims regarding incidents including a cloud component, threats preventable by meeting the top 5 CIS controls, data breaches resulting from employee actions, and new customer environments containing latent threats.

TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT MDR ARCHITECTURE. The scoped environment is stated as 1200 Users, 12,500 Student Users, 100 Servers, 1 300 Series Sensor, and 90 Day Log Retention, using AWN301 sensors and Secure Transport with API and platform integration to the Arctic Wolf Concierge Security Team. Monitored inputs include client monitoring agent and quarantine, firewall/UTM, Active Directory, server logs, anti-virus, Arctic Wolf Agent, DNS logs, HTTP and TLS, wireless APs, Cisco AMP for Endpoints, network monitoring with log collection and NTA, wireless networks, Windows event logs, system vulnerabilities, rootkit/compromise checks, process tables, installed patches, configuration benchmarks, asset information, and cloud monitoring of SaaS and IaaS.

WHY ARCTIC WOLF. Industry framing figures: 3,000 vendors, $120B total spend, and 3,950 reported breaches. Company facts: 1,200+ employees, 3,300+ customers, founded 2012. Audit and compliance drivers named are PCI DSS, FFIEC-NCUA, HIPAA, NIST 800-171, and 23 NYCRR 500. Better Protection statistics: Dwell Time 0:30, with the industry average time to identify an intrusion given as 206 days versus 30 minutes or less for Arctic Wolf; Phishing 18% of customers have phishing activity missed by email security but caught by Arctic Wolf; Advanced Threats 43% of customers have advanced threat activity missed by security tools; Account Takeover 70% of customers have some PII exposure, with 5.5% having plaintext passwords exposed online; and Unpatched Vulnerabilities 35% reduction in time to patch critical vulnerabilities after activating Arctic Wolf. The top five attack vectors listed are malware/ransomware, phishing, PUP adware, account hijacking, and unpatched outdated software. Citing the 2019 Ponemon Cost of Data Breach Incident Report, the deck prints 84 Days Mean Time to Contain (MTTC), 230 Days Mean Time to Identify (MTTI), and 314 DAYS. Citing Gartner, 70% of organizations are unable to process more than 60% of their security data, and the security skills gap through 2020 is given as 1.5M.

SECURITY OPERATIONS SCALE. The platform slide prints approximately 165M observations per week, approximately 765 investigations per week, and approximately 1-2 tickets per week, with an illustrative environment of 450 Users, 150 Servers, and 4 Sensors, flowing through Arctic Wolf Triage, the Concierge Security Team, a data lake and correlation database, threat intelligence and IOCs, and a real-time correlation engine.

SECURITY MONITORING BREAKDOWN. The general observation breakdown is given as Network/IDS 30%, SaaS/O365 15%, Active Directory/Domain Controllers 10%, Firewall 10%, EDR/AV 10%, Arctic Wolf Agent 10%, External Vulnerabilities 5%, Account Takeover 5%, and Other (VPN, Darktrace, Varonis) 5%. A comparison table asserts that NTA is included with the Arctic Wolf sensor while others offer NIDS/HIDS only, that asset inventory across endpoint and network is included, that vulnerability scanning is included, and that integrations, engagement with the CST, remote incident response, security guidance, custom rules, log ingestion and volume, log bandwidth, and security posture reviews are unlimited, with security posture reviews defaulting to once per month.

PRICING PROPOSAL. Arctic Wolf MDR is described as including a fully managed and hosted SIEM, 24x7 monitoring, a named Concierge Security Team, Managed Cloud Monitoring for O365 and Azure, monthly external vulnerability scanning, host-based isolation and managed containment, monthly and quarterly reporting, ad hoc reports on request, unlimited log volume and events per second, 90 days log retention, unlimited custom rules, and managed IDS. Arctic Wolf Service Assurance protects Troy Schools with up to $500,000 in financial assistance for a covered security event, itemized as Compliance $100,000, Ransomware and BEC $100,000, Cyber Legal Liability $250,000, and Business Income $50,000; eligibility requires purchasing MDR and Managed Awareness or Managed Risk and committing to standard terms of an annual contract paid upfront with an 8% annual renewal increase. A separate slide states a multi-year deal with all products is required to qualify for the $1,000,000 level. Arctic Wolf Managed Security Awareness includes a fully managed awareness program, awareness program coaching, multiple integration options, gamification, ongoing microlearning, integrated phishing simulations, 24x7 account takeover monitoring, and performance analytics.

2022_242_board_meeting_power_point_pdf.paragraph: Board presentation on the English Language Arts Curriculum Review and Revision for Grades 9-12 during 2021-2022, laying out the rationale for moving the high school program to a workshop model already used in elementary and middle school. District data on SAT college level reading readiness show Cohort 1 (2016-2018) at 82.47 in 9th grade, 83.50 in 10th, and 76.85 in 11th, a stated decrease of 5.62%, and Cohort 2 (2017-2019) at 86.80, 84.70, and 81.44, a stated decrease of 5.36%. A 9th Grade Curriculum Development Team is writing six workshop-style, skill-based units for piloting in 2022-2023, with a new 9th Grade English course in 2023-2024 and 10th Grade English in 2024-2025.
2022_242_board_meeting_power_point_pdf.page:
**Topic**
ELA Curriculum Review and Revision, Grades 9-12, 2021-2022, presented to the Troy Board of Education.

**Collectively Developed Priorities**
The need to effectively serve ALL students; recent SAT college level reading readiness data meriting consideration; addressing the gap between high and low performing students; adequate training for teachers in advancing readers; a priority placed on the blue and red pillars; protected practice time for reading, writing, and critical thinking; learning environments conducive to responsive teaching; building student independence in college and career readiness skills; a commitment to rich, student-centered discussion and critical thinking; and choice, rigor, and diversity of text selection in all courses.

**District Data: SAT College Level Reading Readiness**

| Cohort | 9th Grade | 10th Grade | 11th Grade | Stated change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cohort 1: 2016-2018 | 82.47 | 83.50 | 76.85 | Decrease of 5.62% |
| Cohort 2: 2017-2019 | 86.80 | 84.70 | 81.44 | Decrease of 5.36% |

**Rationale**
The presentation cites Michael Fullan et al (2006), Breakthrough, for the proposition that the old mission of schools was universal access to basic education plus university access for a small elite, and that whereas twenty years ago 95% of jobs were low-skilled, today those jobs constitute only 10% of the entire economy. The new mission is to get all students to meet high standards and equip them as lifelong learners. Capacities of the literate individual are excerpted from the Michigan Common Core State Standards: demonstrate independence; build strong content knowledge; respond to the varying demands of audience, task, purpose and discipline; comprehend as well as critique; value evidence; use technology and media strategically and capably; and come to understand other perspectives and cultures.

**Course Pathways**
Current trajectory, described as limited options and a linear path: 9 Lit and Comp, 10 Lit and Comp, 11 LC/Elective, 12 Lit and Comp, with an honors strand of 9 LC Honors, 10 LC Honors, 11 AP Language, 12 AP Literature. Preferred future, described as more options with all students prepared for choice: 9th Grade English in 2023-2024 and 10th Grade English in 2024-2025, opening into American Lit, World Lit, AP Language, AP Literature, and Electives.

**Workshop Model Experience**
The literacy journey runs from elementary through middle school to high school, with curricular coherence aligning to Workshop in elementary at 5th and 6th grade. Middle school teachers report that avid readers are plowing through books and reluctant readers are reading more than in past years, that students are writing more daily through jots, long writes and flash drafts, that current students are performing well and challenge themselves with higher level books through book clubs, and that students are more engaged and thinking deeply. Areas for growth identified by middle school colleagues are conferring, resources and professional development, and small group resources and professional development.

**Professional Development**
5 teachers participated in the Teachers College Writing Institute in July 2021. 8 teachers participated in the Teachers College HS Book Club Institute in December 2021. 11 teachers participated in a webinar with Penny Kittle and Kelly Gallagher in December 2021. A full day of PD was provided in August, led by fellow teachers. During the November late start, a TC Staff Developer led PD on using on-demand writing samples to inform small groups and conferring. 9th grade teachers and coaches continue to visit middle school classrooms. Coaches participated in an on-site day with Teachers College in March 2022 and secondary administrators in February 2022, both with TC Staff Developer Natalie Louis.

**Current Work and Next Steps**
A 9th Grade Curriculum Development Team was created, prioritized skills for 9th grade, and outlined skills for all 6 units; the team has met twice to unpack vertical alignment of skills from 6-8, will visit middle school classrooms to observe through the lenses of 3 workshop commitments, and will spend time with a TC Staff Developer in lab settings receiving guidance for Units 1-3. The goal is to write 6 workshop-style, skill-based units to be piloted in 2022-2023. Next steps: summer learning through the Teaching Writing in High School Institute and a Summer Homegrown Institute on Creating Teacher Toolkits to Support a Wide-Range of Writers, followed by targeted piloting of 9th grade units in Fall 2022.

**Ask of the Board**
Target professional development to meet teacher needs, specifically centered around responsive teaching and differentiation at both middle school and high school, and continue to honor the workshop commitment of choice by funding access to fascinating texts.
2022_242_board_meeting_power_point_pdf.verbose:
Board meeting PowerPoint presenting the English Language Arts Curriculum Review and Revision for Grades 9-12 during the 2021-2022 school year in the Troy School District, setting out why the high school ELA program should shift toward the reading and writing workshop model already implemented in the District's elementary and middle schools.

COLLECTIVELY DEVELOPED PRIORITIES. The presentation opens with a list of priorities developed collectively: the need to effectively serve ALL students; recent data in SAT college level reading readiness that merits consideration; addressing the gap between high and low performing students; adequate training for teachers in advancing readers; a priority placed on the blue and red pillars; protected practice time for reading, writing, and critical thinking; learning environments conducive to responsive teaching; building student independence in college and career readiness skills; a commitment to rich, student-centered discussion and critical thinking; and choice, rigor, and diversity of text selection in all courses.

DISTRICT DATA, DECREASE IN SAT COLLEGE LEVEL READING READINESS. Two cohorts are tracked. Cohort 1, spanning 2016-2018, shows 9th Grade 82.47, 10th Grade 83.50, and 11th Grade 76.85, labeled as a Decrease of 5.62%. Cohort 2, spanning 2017-2019, shows 9th Grade 86.80, 10th Grade 84.70, and 11th Grade 81.44, labeled as a Decrease of 5.36%.

RATIONALE AND RESEARCH BASE. The deck quotes the argument that study after study shows globalization and new information technologies have made it especially urgent for schools to chart a new mission. It cites Breakthrough by Michael Fullan and colleagues (2006) for the point that the old mission for schools was to provide universal access to basic education and then to provide a small elite with access to university education. It states that the world has changed: whereas twenty years ago 95% of jobs were low-skilled, today those jobs constitute only 10% of the entire economy. The new mission is described as getting all students to meet high standards of education and providing them with a lifelong education that does not have the built-in obsolescence of so much old-style curriculum but that equips them to be lifelong learners.

STANDARDS FRAMING. Excerpted from the Michigan Common Core State Standards, the presentation lists the capacities of the literate individual that students exhibit with increasing fullness and regularity as they advance through the grades and master the standards in reading, writing, speaking, listening, and language: demonstrate independence; build strong content knowledge; respond to the varying demands of audience, task, purpose and discipline; comprehend as well as critique; value evidence; use technology and media strategically and capably; and come to understand other perspectives and cultures.

CURRENT COURSE TRAJECTORY. The present high school pathway is characterized as limited options on a linear path. The general sequence runs 9 Lit and Comp, 10 Lit and Comp, 11 LC/Elective, and 12 Lit and Comp. The accelerated sequence runs 9 LC Honors, 10 LC Honors, 11 AP Language, and 12 AP Literature.

PREFERRED COURSE STRUCTURE. The preferred model is described as more options with all students prepared for choice. It begins with a redesigned 9th Grade English course in 2023-2024 followed by a redesigned 10th Grade English course in 2024-2025, after which students may select from American Lit, World Lit, AP Language, AP Literature, and Electives.

LITERACY JOURNEY AND CURRICULAR COHERENCE. The presentation traces the literacy journey from elementary to middle school to high school, noting curricular coherence that aligns with Workshop in elementary, with slides addressing 5th Grade and 6th Grade and the movement of Workshop into the middle school.

WHAT THE DISTRICT HAS LEARNED FROM WORKSHOP IN MIDDLE SCHOOL. The stated lessons are that the student is at the center of the work; that skills are at the forefront with content used to achieve those skills; that choice in reading and writing allows for the engagement necessary for growth; that time to practice is the hallmark of the workshop model; and that normalizing feedback in the moment to meet students where they are promotes progress for all.

POSITIVE ASPECTS REPORTED BY MIDDLE SCHOOL TEACHERS. Teachers report that avid readers are plowing through books and reluctant readers are reading more than in past years. Students are writing more, with daily jots, long writes, or flash drafts, and fewer students sit and say they do not know what to write about; notebooks are filled with drafts, revisions, and edits. Current students are performing well, with some challenging themselves through reading higher level books, and teachers report doing a good job encouraging reading more difficult books through book clubs. Students are described as more engaged and thinking deeply about what they are reading.

AREAS FOR GROWTH IDENTIFIED BY MIDDLE SCHOOL COLLEAGUES. Three areas are named: conferring; resources and professional development; and small group resources and professional development.

WHAT TEACHERS NEED AS THE WORK EXTENDS TO HIGH SCHOOL, AND THE ASK OF THE BOARD. The presentation asks the Board to target professional development to meet teacher needs, specifically centered around responsive teaching and differentiation at both the middle school and high school levels, and to continue to honor the workshop commitment of choice by funding access to fascinating texts.

ONGOING SUPPORT FOR TEACHERS THROUGHOUT THE TRANSITION. 5 teachers participated in the Teachers College Writing Institute in July 2021. 8 teachers participated in the Teachers College HS Book Club Institute in December 2021. 11 teachers participated in a webinar with Penny Kittle and Kelly Gallagher in December 2021. A full day of professional development was provided in August and led by fellow teachers. During the November late start, a Teachers College Staff Developer led professional development on how to use on-demand writing samples to inform small groups and conferring. 9th grade teachers and coaches continue to visit middle school classrooms. Coaches participated in an on-site day with Teachers College in March 2022, and secondary administrators participated in an on-site day with Teachers College in February 2022. Teachers shared their learning with the 9-12 ELA team, and teachers learned more about engaging students in writing to increase volume. The Administrators' Day and the Coaches' Day were both conducted with Teachers College Staff Developer Natalie Louis.

CURRENT WORK WITH HIGH SCHOOL. A 9th Grade Curriculum Development Team (CDT) was created. The team prioritized skills for 9th grade and outlined skills for all 6 units. The CDT will visit middle school classrooms to observe through the lenses of the 3 workshop commitments. The stated goal is to write 6 workshop-style, skill-based units that will be piloted in 2022-2023. The team has already met twice to unpack the vertical alignment of skills from grades 6 through 8. The CDT will spend time with a Teachers College Staff Developer in lab settings and receive guidance for Units 1-3. Summer learning for the team includes creating teacher toolkits to support a wide range of writers and a Teaching Writing in High School Institute. A slide is devoted to the 9th Grade CDT's work on vertical alignment of skills.

NEXT STEPS. Summer learning consists of the Teaching Writing in High School Institute and a Summer Homegrown Institute titled Creating Teacher Toolkits to Support a Wide-Range of Writers. For Fall 2022, the next step is targeted piloting of the 9th grade units.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY. Under the strategic initiative Enhance Security and Visibility, the stated problems are that Troy Schools has a distributed network across multiple physical buildings with most traffic backhauled to the central hub, making visibility across the environment and monitoring of network traffic for security relevant perspectives a challenge; that Troy Schools has multiple security tools in place with limited staff to monitor and correlate alerts or identify and respond to potential malicious activity; and that a lack of a broad detection and response mechanism could prevent the ability to quickly identify, contain and remediate sophisticated threats. Desired outcomes are to operationalize a full-feature SIEM solution leveraging existing IT and security controls, a full-functioning cloud-integrated SOC service, and a service-based solution providing quarantine and remediation guidance in real time. The proposed solution is Arctic Wolf's security operations as-a-concierge service ingesting Troy Schools environmental telemetry for 24x7x365 observations, investigations, and incident response guidance; an open, vendor-agnostic SIEM platform ingesting all standardized log sources plus live network traffic analysis; and three dedicated Security Operations FTEs providing proactive threat hunting and continuous improvement.

CURRENT ASSESSMENT. Challenges heard from the Troy team: IT and security resources are constrained and the cost and complexity to build a 24x7x365 cybersecurity team in-house is probably unrealistic; endpoint and network security tools are in place and seasoned security professionals are wanted to guide environmental hardening and continuous improvement; and there is interest in human-led, proactive threat hunting over basic alert-response and typical operational-level services. Negative impacts listed are risk from cyber attack and inability to prevent, detect, respond and remediate quickly; reactive response distracting already burdened IT staff from existing initiatives and projects; and inability to identify dormant vulnerabilities and threats risking a larger and longer-term breach. Business value drivers are Benchmark Your Business, Team Enhancement, Faster Intrusion Detection, and Harden Your Environment.

SERVICE OFFERINGS. Managed Risk (Discover, Benchmark, Harden) is framed by the Center for Internet Security statement that 80% of breaches could have been prevented if the organization had met the top 5 CIS controls. Managed Detection and Response covers Detect, Respond, and Recover. Managed Cloud Monitoring covers Identify, Monitor, and Simplify, including unsecured S3 buckets and unauthorized cloud deployments. Managed Security Awareness covers Engage, Measure, and Transform. The accompanying statistics band prints 47%, 80%, 85% and 70% against claims concerning incidents including a cloud component, threats preventable by meeting the top 5 CIS controls, data breaches resulting from employee actions, and new customer environments containing latent threats.

TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT MDR ARCHITECTURE. The environment is stated as 1200 Users, 12,500 Student Users, 100 Servers, 1 300 Series Sensor, and 90 Day Log Retention, with AWN301 sensors and Secure Transport feeding the Arctic Wolf Concierge Security Team through API and platform integration. WHY ARCTIC WOLF. Industry framing: 3,000 vendors, $120B total spend, 3,950 reported breaches. Company: 1,200+ employees, 3,300+ customers, founded 2012.
